newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel says petrol-tax hike report "speculation".
newsitem.headline: Waigel says petrol-tax hike report "speculation".

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel dismissed as "pure speculation" a report in the Bild-Zeitung newspaper that Germany is considering raising petrol tax by 18 pfennigs per litre from July 1 this year.

Waigel told reporters the coalition is still consulting with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) about tax reform. Chancellor Helmut Kohl is due to meet SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, who favours a petrol-tax rise, on Wednesday.
Waigel said he would also prefer a rise in petrol tax to an increase in value-added tax, if increases are needed to finance cuts in social-security withholdings.
Bild said the petrol tax rise could boost government revenues by 15 billion marks, and would be used to reduce unemployment benefit contributions by one percentage point.
Bild said the reduction in jobless benefit contributions would be a possible concession by the government to the opposition SPD in a protracted dispute over plans for a tax reform.
The SPD has demanded a reduction in non-wage labour costs as a precondition for it agreeing to the tax reform plan, which the government says would relieve taxpayers' burden by 30 billion marks.
Chancellery minister Friedrich Bohl challenged the SPD ahead of Tuesday's talks to present figures on how much it planned to cut taxes.

Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber of the Christian Social Union said he would prefer to see value-added tax increased, as a rise in petrol tax would hurt the automobile industry, which is heavily represented in his state.

Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of the Free Democrats, junior partners in Kohl's coalition, said his party opposes any tax increase. The social security system itself must be reformed to finance the cuts in withholdings, he said.
The government is seeking agreement with the SPD because the opposition can block most tax measures through its control of the upper house of parliament.

The timing of the tax reform, aimed at stimulating investment and jobs creation, is critical as the government tries to trim its budget deficit to meet the strict entry criteria for European monetary union.
